chapter: Films, Las Vegas and the union
title: Jerry Fielding hires Black musicians on The Life of Riley
summary: Callender says Fielding was called a Communist for hiring two Black musicians, and Willard explains how Collette's treatment pushed him to fight for amalgamation.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Then the other ones listed in Meeker's book were the Life of Riley in 1949...
Life of Riley, yeah. That was my first steady show. That was the one with Jerry Fielding.

I mentioned that before, yes. That was about the same time Buddy Collette... Well, it was a little after Buddy was hired to do the Groucho Marx Show. That's when Jerry Fielding really bit off a big chunk when he decided to use two Black musicians on his shows, you know. They thought that... Well, he was called a Communist for doing that. Which was ridiculous, but that was the word, you know. "What right has he to hire Black people, where he's taking work away from good White people?" It wasn't like that at all. He just hired us because he liked the way we played.

I think that was one of the things that led to Buddy's determination to do something about amalgamation. When he found out that the contractor on the show wouldn't give him a W-2 and wouldn't give him...
Yes, he had to go over on Central Avenue to pick up his check or something like that.
He was not treated the same as the other musicians because the contractor was a member of Local 47, and Buddy was 767.
